headline: Context Fatigue Is Real, and /clear Is the Cure
lede: A developer's wry confession — three months of declining AI output, traced finally to a full context window rather than a dumber model — captures something genuine about how large-language-model coding assistants actually work. The discovery of a single command, `/clear`, restored performance. The real story is why that happens, and what else most users are missing.
body:
Every AI coding assistant runs against a hard ceiling called the **context window** — the total number of tokens (roughly, word-fragments) the model can hold in its working memory at once. Claude Code, Anthropic's terminal-based coding agent, is no exception. As a conversation grows — accumulated file reads, error traces, half-finished refactors, earlier questions — the window fills. The model isn't growing worse; it's being asked to reason coherently across an increasingly cluttered table. Old context crowds out fresh signal, and responses can become vaguer, more repetitive, or simply less sharp.

The `/clear` command solves this by wiping the session history and starting a blank conversation. The model's capabilities are unchanged; what changed is the noise-to-signal ratio. This is not a bug so much as a structural property of *transformer* architectures, which attend to all tokens in the window simultaneously — more tokens means more interference from irrelevant material. Power users have long known to clear aggressively; most newcomers don't realize the option exists.

For sessions where history matters but the window is straining, Claude Code offers `/compact` — a middle path that summarizes prior context into a condensed form before continuing, preserving meaningful state without keeping every token verbatim. The image attached to the post reveals other commands: `CLAUDE.md`, a project-level instruction file the model reads on startup; *hooks*, shell commands wired to events like file saves or tool calls; and `--max-budget-usd`, a cost ceiling per session. Each represents a different surface for shaping model behavior rather than fighting it.

The broader lesson the tweet dramatizes is one of *tool literacy* — the gap between using a sophisticated tool as a chatbot that happens to live in the terminal versus actually reading its interface. Claude Code was designed around a command vocabulary. Ignoring that vocabulary and then attributing degraded output to model quality is a pattern that recurs across developer tools: blame the instrument before checking the manual.

None of this is to say context-window limits are a minor inconvenience. For large codebases, they remain a genuine constraint. But the specific frustration the post describes — a slow degradation the user attributed to the model itself — is almost always context saturation, and it's almost always fixable in under three seconds.

concepts.definition: The maximum number of tokens — fragments of text — a language model can process in a single pass. Everything the model 'remembers' during a conversation must fit inside this window. When it fills, older material competes with new input, which can make responses feel less focused or coherent.

A built-in Claude Code command that erases the current conversation history and starts a fresh session. The model's weights and abilities are unchanged; only the accumulated context is discarded, freeing the full window for new work.

A Claude Code command that condenses the existing conversation into a shorter summary before continuing. It preserves meaningful context without keeping every prior token verbatim, offering a middle path between a full /clear and an overloaded session.

A markdown file placed in a project's root directory that Claude Code reads automatically at session start. It lets developers embed standing instructions, conventions, or context into every conversation without repeating them manually.

Shell commands configured to run automatically in response to events inside a Claude Code session — for example, after a file is written or a tool is called. They allow automated, repeatable behaviors without prompting the model each time.

fact_check: The claim that output quality 'doubles' after /clear is anecdotal shorthand, not a measured figure. The underlying observation — that context saturation degrades response quality — is well-documented as a real phenomenon, but the magnitude varies by session length, task type, and model. The framing is vivid rather than precise.
